w: Wrong - denosumab is for giant cell tumour, not Ewing sarcoma.
Wrong - mutilating surgery is not justified when an effective non-surgical option exists.
Wrong - intralesional surgery leaves tumour behind and contaminates the field.
Correct - radiotherapy plus chemotherapy is the standard for unresectable Ewing sarcoma.
Wrong - chemotherapy alone without local control gives unacceptable recurrence.

mcq.stem:
A 9-year-old boy fell onto his outstretched hand and now has pain in the upper arm. He had no symptoms before. X-ray shows a central, well-defined lucent lesion in the proximal humeral metaphysis abutting the physis, with a thinned cortex and a transverse fracture; a small cortical fragment lies in the dependent part of the lesion.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: A central metaphyseal lucent lesion of the proximal humerus in a child, found after a pathological fracture, is a simple (unicameral) bone cyst. The cortical fragment that has sunk to the dependent part of the fluid-filled cavity is the ‘fallen fragment’ sign, which is pathognomonic. A solid tumour cannot let a fragment fall through it.
w: Wrong - GCT occurs after skeletal maturity and is epiphyseal.
Wrong - ABC is eccentric, more expansile and blood-filled; fragments do not ‘fall’.
Wrong - fibrous dysplasia gives a ground-glass lesion and shepherd's crook deformity.
Correct - central proximal humeral cyst with a fallen fragment = simple bone cyst.
Wrong - telangiectatic osteosarcoma is aggressive with a wide zone of transition and cortical destruction.

mcq.stem:
A 10-year-old girl has an undisplaced pathological fracture through a central, well-defined, fluid-filled cyst of the proximal humeral metaphysis showing a fallen fragment sign. Her arm is otherwise neurovascularly intact.
What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Urgent curettage, bone grafting and locking plate
Sling until the fracture heals, then reassess the cyst
En bloc resection with endoprosthetic replacement
Core biopsy followed by neoadjuvant chemotherapy
Polidocanol sclerotherapy as an inpatient tomorrow
mcq.e: Most pathological fractures through a simple bone cyst of the upper limb unite with a sling, and some cysts heal after fracture. Persistent active cysts are then treated with aspiration and methylprednisolone injection, or curettage and grafting if that fails or the fracture is displaced. Weight-bearing sites such as the proximal femur more often need fixation.
w: Wrong - surgery is reserved for displaced fractures, weight-bearing sites or failed injection.
Correct - non-weight-bearing limb: immobilise, let the fracture heal, then reassess the cyst.
Wrong - this is a benign cyst; en bloc resection is grossly excessive.
Wrong - the appearance is diagnostic of a benign cyst; chemotherapy is not indicated.
Wrong - polidocanol sclerotherapy is a treatment for aneurysmal bone cyst.

mcq.stem:
A 14-year-old girl has 4 months of progressive pain and swelling over the distal tibia. X-ray shows an eccentric, expansile, ‘blown-out’ lytic lesion of the metaphysis with a thin cortical shell. MRI shows multiple septated cavities with fluid-fluid levels.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Sclerotherapy straight away without any tissue diagnosis
Reassurance and a repeat radiograph in 12 months
Methylprednisolone injection as for a unicameral cyst
Skeletal survey and SPEP to look for myeloma
mcq.e: These features suggest an aneurysmal bone cyst, but fluid-fluid levels are not specific: telangiectatic osteosarcoma, GCT with secondary ABC change and other lesions can look identical. Diagnosis of ABC must therefore be confirmed by biopsy before treatment. Missing a telangiectatic osteosarcoma would be catastrophic.
w: Correct - biopsy is required to confirm ABC and exclude telangiectatic osteosarcoma.
Wrong - treating without histology risks missing a malignant mimic.
Wrong - a growing, painful expansile lesion needs diagnosis and treatment, not delay.
Wrong - steroid injection is for simple bone cysts; this lesion is an eccentric blood-filled cyst.
Wrong - myeloma does not occur in a 14-year-old.

mcq.stem:
A 16-year-old boy has a painful, expanding lesion of the proximal fibula. Biopsy confirms a primary aneurysmal bone cyst with no malignant or giant cell tumour component. There is no fracture and the common peroneal nerve is functioning normally.
What is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: External beam radiotherapy as first-line therapy
Aggressive curettage with adjuvant and bone graft
Observation, as it heals spontaneously after fracture
Single methylprednisolone injection into the cyst
mcq.e: Symptomatic aneurysmal bone cysts are treated with aggressive (extended) curettage, often with an adjuvant such as a high-speed burr, phenol or cryotherapy, and bone grafting. Sclerotherapy (e.g. polidocanol) and selective arterial embolisation are alternatives, especially in the spine or pelvis. Recurrence occurs in up to 20%.
w: Wrong - radiotherapy risks sarcoma and growth disturbance and is avoided in benign lesions.
Wrong - ABC is benign; chemotherapy and wide resection are not indicated.
Correct - extended curettage with adjuvant and grafting is the standard for symptomatic ABC.
Wrong - spontaneous healing after fracture is a feature of some simple bone cysts, not ABC.
Wrong - steroid injection is a simple bone cyst treatment.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old man has 3 months of back pain, fatigue and recurrent chest infections. Hb is 8.9 g/dL, corrected calcium 3.0 mmol/L and creatinine 210 µmol/L. Total protein is high with low albumin. A skull X-ray shows multiple small punched-out lytic lesions.
Which investigation is most useful to confirm the diagnosis?
o: CT-guided biopsy of a lytic skull lesion
Serum PTH and vitamin D levels
mcq.e: Anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, lytic bone lesions (CRAB), infections and a high globulin gap point to multiple myeloma. SPEP/UPEP (with immunofixation and serum free light chains) demonstrate the monoclonal paraprotein, and bone marrow biopsy confirms clonal plasma cells. Bone scan is often falsely negative.
w: Wrong - myeloma lesions are purely lytic, so bone scans are often cold or falsely negative.
Correct - SPEP/UPEP identify the monoclonal M-protein and Bence Jones protein.
Wrong - PSA looks for prostate cancer, which gives sclerotic metastases.
Wrong - biopsying a skull lesion is unnecessary; electrophoresis and marrow biopsy are less invasive and diagnostic.
Wrong - PTH explains hypercalcaemia from hyperparathyroidism but not anaemia, renal failure and a globulin gap.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old woman has newly diagnosed multiple myeloma confirmed on bone marrow biopsy, with an IgG paraprotein. She has back and rib pain. A junior doctor requests a technetium bone scan to map her skeletal disease.
Which imaging is most appropriate to assess her bone disease?
mcq.e: Myeloma suppresses osteoblasts while activating osteoclasts, so lesions are purely lytic with no reactive bone formation; bone scans are therefore often cold or falsely negative. Whole-body low-dose CT (or a skeletal survey, MRI or PET-CT) is used to detect lytic lesions, fractures and areas at risk of fracture.
w: Correct - whole-body low-dose CT is more sensitive than a skeletal survey and is now preferred.
Wrong - ultrasound cannot survey the skeleton for lytic lesions.
Wrong - bone scan relies on osteoblastic activity and frequently misses myeloma lesions.
Wrong - a chest X-ray alone misses spine, pelvis and limb lesions.
Wrong - DEXA measures bone density, not focal lytic lesions.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old man with multiple myeloma has widespread lytic lesions on whole-body CT, including a vertebral collapse. Curiously, his serum ALP is normal and an earlier bone scan was reported as normal.
What is the best explanation for these findings?
o: Paraprotein binding the tracer within the blood
Lesions too small to be resolved by gamma camera
Renal impairment reducing tracer delivery to bone
mcq.e: Myeloma cells activate the RANKL pathway, increasing osteoclastic resorption, and also inhibit osteoblasts (e.g. via DKK1). Without osteoblastic repair, ALP stays normal and technetium bone scans, which depend on osteoblastic activity, are often negative. This is why skeletal survey, low-dose CT, MRI or PET-CT are used instead.
w: Wrong - paraprotein does not bind bone-scan tracer.
Wrong - many myeloma lesions are large; the issue is the lack of osteoblastic response, not size.
Wrong - renal impairment would, if anything, increase background activity, not abolish lesion uptake.
Wrong - there is no hepatic dysfunction; ALP is normal because osteoblasts are suppressed.
Correct - uncoupled bone turnover (osteoclasts on, osteoblasts off) explains normal ALP and a cold bone scan.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man with renal cell carcinoma has an ache in his right upper arm, moderate in severity, not limited to activity. X-ray shows a purely lytic lesion in the humeral diaphysis destroying about half of the cortical diameter.
What is his Mirels' score?
mcq.e: Mirels' score adds site (upper limb 1, lower limb 2, peritrochanteric 3), pain (mild 1, moderate 2, functional 3), lesion type (blastic 1, mixed 2, lytic 3) and size as a fraction of cortical diameter (under 1/3 = 1, 1/3-2/3 = 2, over 2/3 = 3). Here: upper limb 1 + moderate 2 + lytic 3 + half 2 = 8, a borderline score needing clinical judgement. Note: slide writes ‘Mirel's’; correct is Mirels'.
w: Wrong - this undercounts; check that lytic scores 3 and 1/3-2/3 scores 2.
Wrong - one point short; moderate pain scores 2.
Correct - 1 (upper limb) + 2 (moderate) + 3 (lytic) + 2 (1/3-2/3) = 8.
Wrong - 9 would require functional pain or a lower-limb site.
Wrong - 10 overcounts; upper limb lesions score only 1 for site.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has right hip pain that is worst when walking. X-ray shows a mixed lytic-sclerotic lesion in the subtrochanteric (peritrochanteric) femur involving more than two-thirds of the cortical diameter. There is no fracture.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Bisphosphonate infusion and review in 3 months
Radiotherapy now, fixation only if it fractures
Strict non-weight-bearing on crutches and analgesia
mcq.e: Her Mirels' score is 3 (peritrochanteric) + 3 (functional pain) + 2 (mixed) + 3 (over 2/3) = 11. A score of 9 or more indicates a high fracture risk (about 33% at 9, rising steeply), so prophylactic fixation, here an intramedullary nail protecting the whole femur, is done before radiotherapy. Fixing an impending fracture is safer and gives better function than treating a completed one.
w: Wrong - bisphosphonates reduce skeletal events but do not prevent an imminent fracture.
Wrong - radiotherapy alone is for scores of 7 or less.
Correct - Mirels 11: prophylactic intramedullary fixation followed by radiotherapy.
Wrong - waiting for fracture gives worse outcomes; radiotherapy also weakens bone before healing.
Wrong - non-weight-bearing is impractical and does not address the high fracture risk.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old man with known metastatic renal cell carcinoma has an impending pathological fracture from a large lytic lesion of the proximal femur. He is scheduled for resection and endoprosthetic replacement.
Which preoperative step most reduces the risk of life-threatening intraoperative haemorrhage?
mcq.e: Renal and thyroid metastases are typically lytic and highly vascular, and surgery on them can cause torrential bleeding. Selective preoperative arterial embolisation, ideally within 24-48 hours of surgery, significantly reduces blood loss. Bone-modifying agents and radiotherapy do not reduce acute vascularity enough.
w: Correct - preoperative embolisation is used for hypervascular renal and thyroid metastases.
Wrong - radiotherapy does not rapidly reduce tumour vascularity and impairs wound healing.
Wrong - denosumab reduces skeletal events but does not reduce surgical bleeding.
Wrong - bisphosphonates reduce osteoclast activity but not tumour vascularity.
Wrong - sensible, but tumour hypervascularity is the main bleeding risk here.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man with no history of cancer has 2 months of thigh pain on walking. X-ray shows a solitary lytic lesion of the femoral diaphysis with endosteal erosion of two-thirds of the cortex. A junior surgeon proposes intramedullary nailing on today's list and sending the reamings for histology.
What is the most appropriate course of action?
o: Proceed with nailing and send the reamings
Radiotherapy to the lesion before any tests
Staging work-up and biopsy before fixation
Bone scan, then nail if no other lesion
mcq.e: A solitary bone lesion without a known primary may be a primary bone sarcoma rather than a metastasis. Intramedullary nailing would contaminate the whole femoral canal and soft tissues, potentially converting a limb-salvage case into amputation. Full staging (bloods including SPEP and PSA, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, bone scan) and a planned biopsy must come first.
w: Wrong - nailing an undiagnosed solitary lesion spreads a possible sarcoma along the canal.
Wrong - irradiating without a diagnosis is inappropriate and could be the wrong treatment.
Correct - stage and biopsy first; a solitary lesion must be proven metastatic before fixation.
Wrong - amputation without a diagnosis is never justified.
Wrong - a negative bone scan does not exclude a primary sarcoma; tissue is still needed.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has had 3 weeks of worsening mid-back pain, worse when lying flat. Today he has bilateral leg heaviness and numbness below the umbilicus. Bladder function is normal. Plain X-rays show sclerotic lesions in several thoracic and lumbar vertebrae.
What is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Urgent MRI of the lumbar spine only
Technetium bone scan within a week
Urgent MRI of the whole spine
Nerve conduction studies of the legs
mcq.e: Back pain with new leg weakness and a sensory level in a patient with cancer is metastatic spinal cord compression, an oncological emergency. Urgent MRI of the WHOLE spine is required because compression is often multilevel; dexamethasone is started and spinal surgery and/or radiotherapy is planned. Treatment before sphincter loss gives the best outcome.
w: Wrong - CT abdomen/pelvis does not assess the spinal cord.
Wrong - a sensory level at the umbilicus suggests a thoracic lesion, and multilevel disease is common.
Wrong - a bone scan is too slow and does not show cord compression.
Correct - urgent whole-spine MRI defines all levels of compression.
Wrong - nerve conduction studies do not assess cord compression and delay treatment.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old man has diffuse bone pain and lower urinary tract symptoms. Bloods show raised ALP with normal calcium. X-rays show multiple dense, well-circumscribed sclerotic lesions throughout the pelvis and lumbar spine.
Which blood test is most likely to identify the primary tumour?
mcq.e: Multiple osteoblastic (sclerotic) metastases in an elderly man are most commonly from prostate cancer, about 90% of whose bone metastases are blastic. A markedly raised PSA supports the diagnosis. Breast cancer is the other common source of blastic or mixed deposits; kidney, thyroid and lung metastases are usually lytic.
w: Wrong - CA-125 is an ovarian marker and irrelevant in a man.
Wrong - CEA is mainly a colorectal marker; colorectal bone metastases are uncommon.
Correct - prostate cancer gives sclerotic metastases; PSA is the key marker.
Wrong - AFP is raised in hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumours.
Wrong - thyroid metastases are lytic and hypervascular, not sclerotic.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man has noticed a painless lump at the back of his thigh that has grown over 4 months. Examination shows a firm 7 cm mass that becomes less mobile when he contracts his hamstrings. The GP plans to excise it in the clinic under local anaesthetic as a ‘probable lipoma’.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ultrasound and reassure if it looks fatty
Fine-needle aspiration in the GP clinic
Review again in 6 months for any growth
mcq.e: This mass has red flags for sarcoma: over 5 cm, deep to fascia (fixed on muscle contraction) and enlarging. It needs MRI and referral to a sarcoma centre, where a planned core biopsy is performed, before any excision. An unplanned ‘whoops’ excision contaminates tissue planes and may necessitate far larger surgery.
w: Correct - MRI and urgent referral to a sarcoma centre before any surgery.
Wrong - excising a possible sarcoma without imaging is a ‘whoops’ excision.
Wrong - ultrasound cannot exclude a deep liposarcoma; reassurance would be unsafe.
Wrong - FNA is unreliable for sarcoma and an unplanned track can contaminate tissue.
Wrong - a growing deep mass over 5 cm should not be watched.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man has a 14 cm slowly enlarging, painless mass deep in the anterior thigh. MRI shows a predominantly fatty intramuscular mass with thick, irregular enhancing septa and nodular non-fatty components.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: A large deep fatty mass in the thigh of an adult with thick enhancing septa and nodular non-fatty areas suggests an atypical lipomatous tumour / well-differentiated liposarcoma rather than a lipoma. Simple lipomas are homogeneously fatty with thin septa. Diagnosis is confirmed by core biopsy (MDM2 amplification, lecturer pearl), and treatment is wide excision.
w: Wrong - lipomas are homogeneously fatty without thick septa or nodules.
Wrong - haemangiomas contain serpiginous vessels and phleboliths rather than nodular septa.
Correct - deep, large, fatty mass with thick septa and nodules = liposarcoma (ALT/WDLPS).
Wrong - desmoids are fibrous, infiltrative masses without significant fat.
Wrong - myxofibrosarcoma is myxoid and usually subcutaneous in the elderly, not fatty.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman who had a colectomy for familial adenomatous polyposis has a firm, painless, infiltrative 6 cm mass in the rectus abdominis. Core biopsy shows bland spindle-shaped fibroblasts in abundant collagen with nuclear beta-catenin staining and no atypia. Serial MRI over 6 months shows no growth and she is asymptomatic.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Wide excision with 2 cm margins urgently
mcq.e: Desmoid-type fibromatosis is locally aggressive and infiltrative but never metastasises. Recurrence after surgery is around 50%, and many lesions stabilise or regress spontaneously, so asymptomatic stable desmoids are managed with active surveillance. Symptomatic or progressive lesions are treated with NSAIDs, tamoxifen, chemotherapy, radiotherapy or surgery.
w: Wrong - radiotherapy is not first-line in a young, asymptomatic patient.
Wrong - radical surgery causes morbidity and desmoids often recur regardless.
Wrong - chemotherapy is reserved for progressive or symptomatic disease.
Correct - asymptomatic, stable desmoid: active surveillance.
Wrong - urgent wide excision is not needed for a stable, non-metastasising lesion.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man has a slowly enlarging, violaceous, firm plaque on his upper back that has developed raised nodules over 5 years. Biopsy shows uniform spindle cells in a storiform (cartwheel) pattern, infiltrating subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern.
Which immunohistochemical marker is most likely to be positive?
mcq.e: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is a low-grade, locally aggressive dermal sarcoma with storiform spindle cells that infiltrate fat in a honeycomb pattern and are CD34 positive. Benign dermatofibroma is factor XIIIa positive and CD34 negative. Treatment is wide excision or Mohs surgery, as inadequate excision gives about 50% recurrence.
w: Wrong - CD99 is the Ewing sarcoma marker.
Correct - DFSP is CD34 positive.
Wrong - S100 marks neural tumours (schwannoma) and melanoma.
Wrong - desmin marks muscle tumours (rhabdo- and leiomyosarcoma).
Wrong - factor XIIIa marks benign dermatofibroma, the main mimic.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old woman has years of severe, stabbing pain under her right thumbnail, triggered by minor knocks and by cold water. There is a 3 mm bluish spot beneath the nail plate. Pressing with a pinhead over the spot reproduces exquisite pain, and the pain disappears when the arm is exsanguinated and a tourniquet inflated.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: The triad of paroxysmal pain, pinpoint tenderness and cold intolerance with a bluish subungual spot is classic for glomus tumour. Love's pin test (pinpoint pressure reproduces pain) and Hildreth's tourniquet test (ischaemia abolishes pain) support the diagnosis. MRI confirms it and excision is curative.
w: Wrong - subungual melanoma is pigmented (longitudinal band) and usually painless.
Wrong - pyogenic granuloma is a red, friable, bleeding lesion, not a painful blue spot.
Wrong - subungual exostosis is a bony outgrowth seen on X-ray, usually of the great toe.
Wrong - mucous cysts are translucent swellings near the DIP joint, not painful blue spots.
Correct - triad plus positive Love and Hildreth tests = glomus tumour.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man has had four episodes of atraumatic swelling of the right knee over 2 years. Aspirates showed brown, blood-stained fluid each time. Clotting screen and factor levels are normal. MRI shows nodular synovial thickening throughout the joint with low signal on T2 and ‘blooming’ on gradient echo sequences.
What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
mcq.e: Recurrent atraumatic haemarthrosis with haemosiderin ‘blooming’ on gradient echo MRI and normal clotting indicates diffuse pigmented villonodular synovitis (tenosynovial giant cell tumour). Note: slide spells ‘villonodullar’; correct is villonodular. Total synovectomy (arthroscopic or open) is the gold standard; diffuse disease recurs often, and radiotherapy or CSF1R tyrosine kinase inhibitors are adjuncts.
w: Wrong - symptomatic treatment allows progressive joint destruction.
Wrong - nodule excision suits localised PVNS; diffuse disease would recur.
Wrong - steroid injection does not remove the proliferative synovium.
Wrong - clotting factors are normal, so haemophilia is excluded.
Correct - total synovectomy is the gold standard for diffuse PVNS.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old woman has a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging, mildly painful mass in the popliteal fossa, separate from the knee joint. X-ray shows a soft tissue mass with small peripheral calcifications. MRI shows a heterogeneous lesion with septations and fluid levels. Biopsy shows a biphasic spindle and epithelial cell tumour.
Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
mcq.e: A periarticular soft tissue mass near the knee in a young adult, with calcification and a biphasic histology, is synovial sarcoma. It is defined by t(X;18)(p11;q11), producing the SS18-SSX fusion. Despite its name it does not arise from synovium, and it is one of the sarcomas that can spread to lymph nodes.
w: Wrong - t(17;22) COL1A1-PDGFB is dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.
Wrong - t(11;22) EWSR1-FLI1 is Ewing sarcoma.
Wrong - t(12;16) FUS-DDIT3 is myxoid liposarcoma.
Correct - t(X;18) SS18-SSX defines synovial sarcoma.
Wrong - t(2;13) PAX3-FOXO1 is alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old woman has a slowly growing 3 cm lump on the medial side of her upper arm. Tapping it causes tingling into the ring and little fingers. The lump moves side to side but not along the line of the arm. MRI shows a well-encapsulated, eccentric fusiform mass displacing the ulnar nerve fascicles to one side.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Nerve segment resection with sural graft
Wide excision with a 2 cm margin
Observation, as it cannot be operated
mcq.e: An encapsulated, eccentric nerve sheath tumour that displaces fascicles is a schwannoma. Because it sits beside rather than within the fascicles, it can be shelled out (enucleated) under magnification while preserving nerve function. A neurofibroma is central, with fascicles running through it, so excision usually sacrifices the nerve.
w: Wrong - resecting and grafting the nerve is unnecessary for an eccentric benign schwannoma.
Correct - schwannomas are eccentric and can be enucleated, sparing the nerve.
Wrong - wide excision would sacrifice the ulnar nerve for a benign lesion.
Wrong - radiotherapy is not used for benign peripheral schwannomas.
Wrong - symptomatic schwannomas are readily and safely excised.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old man with neurofibromatosis type 1 has a long-standing plexiform neurofibroma in the posterior thigh. Over 2 months it has enlarged rapidly, causes severe pain at rest, and he has developed weakness of ankle dorsiflexion.
Which investigation best identifies malignant change and guides biopsy?
mcq.e: A rapidly enlarging, painful neurofibroma with new neurological deficit in NF1 suggests a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour, the leading cause of death in NF1. MRI shows the extent, and FDG PET-CT identifies the metabolically active (malignant) part of a large plexiform lesion to target biopsy. Treatment is wide resection with radiotherapy.
w: Correct - FDG PET-CT highlights malignant areas within plexiform neurofibromas.
Wrong - ultrasound cannot reliably distinguish benign from malignant nerve sheath tumours.
Wrong - plain radiographs give little information about soft tissue nerve tumours.
Wrong - nerve conduction studies confirm deficit but not malignancy.
Wrong - bone scans assess the skeleton, not soft tissue nerve tumours.

mcq.stem:
A 6-year-old boy has a rapidly enlarging, painless swelling of the forearm noticed 6 weeks ago. There is no history of trauma, and he is afebrile. MRI shows a soft tissue mass within the forearm muscles without bone involvement. Biopsy shows small round blue cells that stain positive for desmin and myogenin.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the commonest soft tissue sarcoma of childhood. It is a small round blue cell tumour of skeletal muscle lineage, so it is desmin and myogenin positive. Embryonal type affects young children (head and neck, genitourinary), while alveolar type affects limbs in adolescents. Biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis.
w: Wrong - synovial sarcoma occurs in young adults with t(X;18) and is not myogenin positive.
Wrong - Ewing sarcoma is CD99 positive and usually arises in bone.
Wrong - neuroblastoma is a tumour of neural crest origin, not myogenin positive.
Wrong - lymphoma is CD45/leucocyte-marker positive, not myogenin positive.
Correct - desmin and myogenin positivity defines skeletal muscle lineage: rhabdomyosarcoma.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man had a 6 cm lump on his thigh shelled out at a private clinic as a ‘lipoma’, without prior imaging. Histology now shows high-grade myxofibrosarcoma reaching the excision margins at several points. The wound has healed.
What is the most appropriate next management?
o: Staging, then wide re-excision of the tumour bed
Reassurance, as the tumour has been removed
Repeat local excision of only the visible scar
mcq.e: This is a ‘whoops’ excision: an unplanned marginal or intralesional removal of a sarcoma. Residual tumour is likely in the contaminated field, and myxofibrosarcoma is notorious for infiltrative margins and local recurrence. Management at a sarcoma centre is MRI and CT chest staging, then wide re-excision of the whole operative bed, usually with radiotherapy.
w: Correct - stage, then wide re-excision of the contaminated tumour bed (± radiotherapy).
Wrong - positive margins mean residual tumour; reassurance is unsafe.
Wrong - chemotherapy alone does not achieve local control of myxofibrosarcoma.
Wrong - the whole contaminated operative field, not just the scar, must be removed widely.
Wrong - surveillance alone leaves residual high-grade tumour untreated.
